# REPORT_M1

The three measurements of SPEC §M1.10. Every number below was printed by `bench/report_m1.py`. The script runs each command twice and stops if the counters differ, so all numbers are deterministic.

**How to reproduce:** build (see `README.md`), then from the repo root run `python bench/report_m1.py`. All data is generated by the script: CSV files are fixed, and the synthetic traces use seed 3005. The script also checks that the spec's worked trace `1 2 3 1 4 2` at B = 3 gives LRU 1/5/2 and CLOCK 2/4/1 before it measures anything.

## Assumptions: schemas, data and traces

The instructor will not post the M1 trace files or sample data, and asked us to use our own inputs and document them (Brightspace, 2026-11-11). These inputs are final.

- **Capacity tables:** three schemas, each loaded with 1000 copies of one row (section 1): `a:INT,b:INT,c:INT` with `1,2,3`; `a:INT,b:VARCHAR(20),c:INT` with `42,bob,7`; `a:INT,b:VARCHAR(200)` with `1,` and 200 × `x`.
- **Traces** (section 2): five files of page ids, one per line, written by the script (random choices use seed 3005).
  - trace 1: 1000 requests, uniform random over pages 0–199;
  - trace 2: 1000 requests, 80 % to the 40 hot pages 0–39 (20 % of 200), 20 % to pages 40–199;
  - trace 3: pages 0–79 scanned 10 times, 800 requests (exactly the spec's trace 3, §M1.10);
  - trace 4: pages 0–39 looped 25 times, 1000 requests;
  - trace 5: five rounds of a scan of pages 0–99 followed by 100 random lookups in the 20 hot pages 300–319, 1000 requests.
- **Scan table** (section 3): `a:INT,b:INT,c:INT`, rows `i,i,i` for i = 0 … 127 499 (exactly 500 data pages).

## 1. Capacity

The computed value is `floor(4088 / (L + 4))` (§M1.4): 4088 usable bytes per page, and each record costs its L bytes plus a 4-byte slot. The measured value is `slot_count` of page 1 (`storage layout --page 1 --json`) after loading 1000 rows.

| Schema | Row loaded | L (bytes) | Computed | Measured |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `a:INT,b:INT,c:INT` | `1,2,3` | 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 | 255 | 255 |
| `a:INT,b:VARCHAR(20),c:INT` | `42,bob,7` | 4 + (2 + 3) + 4 = 13 | 240 | 240 |
| `a:INT,b:VARCHAR(200)` | `1,` + 200 × `x` | 4 + (2 + 200) = 206 | 19 | 19 |

**Difference: none.** Every row has the same length, so every record costs exactly L + 4 bytes and the formula is exact. The page simply stops when the next record no longer fits. For VARCHAR(200), 19 × 210 = 3990 bytes are used and 98 bytes stay empty, because a 20th record would need 210. With rows of different lengths, the formula would only be an estimate: one fixed L no longer describes the page.

## 2. Policies

Hit rate = hits / requests. Every row satisfies hits + misses = trace length, reads = misses and writes = 0.

The traces are described under Assumptions. Trace 3 is the spec's own; the other four are our access patterns, chosen to cover random access, a hot set, a loop that fits at B = 64, and scans mixed with lookups.

**Trace 3 at B = 64: LRU gets 0 hits out of 800 (0 %).** The scan cycles through 80 pages, but only 64 fit, so each time a new page is loaded LRU evicts the least recently used page, which is exactly the page the scan will ask for soonest. Every request therefore finds its page just evicted (sequential flooding), and memory only starts to help once all 80 pages fit (B = 256: only the first 80 requests miss, 90 %). CLOCK does the same here: with a cyclic scan every reference bit is set, so the sweep clears them all and evicts the oldest page, just as LRU does.

**Which policy we ship: LRU** (already the default in every tool). On these traces it is equal to or slightly better than CLOCK in every row but one (trace5 at B = 4: 103 vs 105 hits), and its victim is easy to explain and check by hand. CLOCK's advantage, a cheaper bookkeeping step on every hit, does not change any counter in this project. Neither policy fixes sequential flooding; that would need a scan-resistant policy such as LRU-K (O'Neil et al.) or MRU for scans.

## 3. Scan cost

A table of exactly 500 data pages: `a:INT,b:INT,c:INT`, 127 500 rows (255 per page), listed by one directory page. Counters from `storage scan --frames B --json`.

| B | Reads | Hits | Misses | Evictions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 501 | 0 | 501 | 500 |
| 8 | 501 | 0 | 501 | 494 |
| 64 | 501 | 0 | 501 | 438 |

**Reads are 501 at every B, as expected:** 500 data pages plus 1 directory page, each read once. The number does not fall as B grows, because a scan never comes back to a page it has finished, so a bigger pool has nothing useful to keep. It does not rise either. The scan pins one page at a time and fetches each page exactly once: it reads the directory page, notes its entry count, unpins it, then visits data pages 1 … 500 by number (entry i of directory page d is always data page d + 1 + i). So there are no hits. (Re-measured 2026-11-07 after this change; an earlier version fetched the directory page again before every data page, which gave 500 hits here, but a second disk read per page when a blocking exec operator left the scan only one frame.) Evictions are 501 minus the free frames: one frame already holds catalog page 0 from opening the database, so B = 8 has 7 free frames (501 − 7 = 494) and B = 64 has 63 (501 − 63 = 438).
